scenes.title: The baggage on the road
scenes.caption: Pack animals carried food, tools and spare equipment behind the fighting troops. A campaign that would reach the Indus began with the ordinary work of loading bundles and keeping a long column moving.

scenes.title: Preparing the long spears
scenes.caption: Macedonian infantry fought in close ranks with long sarissas. Before a march, men would have checked wooden shafts, metal fittings and shield straps; the effectiveness of the formation depended on equipment as much as drill.

scenes.title: The opposite bank
scenes.caption: At the Granicus, the approach to the far bank mattered as much as the water itself. Arrian describes cavalry trying to gain footing while Persian horsemen held the higher ground opposite them.

scenes.title: The knot on the wagon
scenes.caption: The famous knot fastened a wagon's yoke to its pole. Ancient accounts disagree about how Alexander released it: the sword stroke is one version, while another describes him removing a fastening pin.

scenes.title: Mountains beside the sea
scenes.caption: The ground near Issus squeezed the armies between the mountains and the Mediterranean. From the coastal plain, the steep slopes and narrow river crossings help explain why Darius could not use his larger army as freely as he wished.

scenes.title: A road into the water
scenes.caption: Timber and stone went into the causeway towards Tyre. As work reached deeper water, the builders faced a harder task and greater exposure to attacks from the island's walls and ships.

scenes.title: Ships under the walls
scenes.caption: The siege changed when fleets from Phoenicia and Cyprus joined Alexander. Ships could block the harbours and bring siege equipment against the seaward walls, adding an approach the causeway alone could not provide.

scenes.title: Marking a future city
scenes.caption: Alexander chose places for streets, sanctuaries and the market on the Egyptian coast. Arrian preserves a story that the builders used grain to mark out the walls when they had nothing suitable for scoring the ground.

scenes.title: Green ground in the desert
scenes.caption: The approach to Ammon's sanctuary ended in an oasis surrounded by desert. Water and cultivated ground made this a place where people could live, receive travellers and maintain a shrine far from the Nile valley.

scenes.title: At the sanctuary of Ammon
scenes.caption: The oracle mattered to Alexander as a place of divine authority. Arrian says that he heard an answer pleasing to him, but does not give a dependable transcript of the private consultation.

scenes.title: Room to manoeuvre
scenes.caption: Darius selected open ground at Gaugamela and had obstacles removed for his chariots. The broad plain gave cavalry room to move, making the direction and timing of each advance especially important.

scenes.title: Through the city gate
scenes.caption: Babylon presented the army with a different scale of urban life. Glazed brick, broad approaches and massive defensive walls belonged to a city whose buildings and institutions had developed long before the Macedonians arrived.

scenes.title: Fields supplied by canals
scenes.caption: Around Babylon, channels carried river water into cultivated land. An army passing through this plain depended on the same grain, water and transport networks that supported the people living there.

scenes.title: Under the palace columns
scenes.caption: Persepolis had received delegations from across the Persian empire. Its high columns, carved stairways and large reception spaces gave the Macedonians a physical view of the royal power they were taking over.

scenes.title: After the palace fire
scenes.caption: Arrian records that Alexander burned the royal palace despite Parmenion's objections. The destruction removed more than a symbol of kingship: timber roofs and the rooms beneath them could not be recovered once the fire had passed.

scenes.title: Changing the pace of pursuit
scenes.caption: At Ecbatana, Alexander reorganised his forces and sent some allied troops home. The pursuit of Darius continued eastwards, with fresh horses and a lighter column becoming more useful than the full weight of an army.

scenes.title: A city at the crossing of routes
scenes.caption: Bactra stood within a settled landscape of cultivation and trade. The army's arrival brought it into contact with communities whose roads, stores and local knowledge mattered as much as the fortress walls.

scenes.title: Crossing without timber
scenes.caption: On the march north from Bactra, the Oxus was difficult to bridge. Arrian describes hides filled with dry material and sewn shut, allowing the army to improvise floats where suitable timber was scarce.

scenes.title: Beyond the garrison
scenes.caption: Holding Maracanda did not mean controlling the surrounding country. Irrigated fields, villages and routes through the valleys sustained communities that continued to resist Macedonian rule under Spitamenes.

scenes.title: Building a frontier town
scenes.caption: Arrian describes the new settlement on the Jaxartes as both a base and a barrier. Soldiers no longer fit for service joined other settlers there, while the army built defences beside a river separating it from mobile groups on the far bank.

scenes.title: Through the older town
scenes.caption: The Taxila of Alexander's day belonged to the settlement now called Bhir Mound. Its narrow streets and houses formed an older urban landscape, centuries before the monasteries and planned cities that survive elsewhere around Taxila.

scenes.title: Provisioning the visitors
scenes.caption: The ruler of Taxila supplied animals, money and other gifts to Alexander. Receiving an army was also a practical problem: food had to be gathered, loads counted and people assigned to move them.

scenes.title: The crossing in the rain
scenes.caption: Alexander repeatedly moved men along the river to confuse Porus about where he would cross. The eventual passage took place upstream during stormy weather, using boats and floats while much of the army remained opposite the Indian camp.

scenes.title: Elephants across the field
scenes.caption: Porus placed elephants along the front of his army, with infantry in the spaces between them. Their size and effect on horses made them a tactical problem very different from the Persian cavalry the Macedonians had fought farther west.

scenes.title: Men who would go no farther
scenes.caption: At the Hyphasis, the soldiers' exhaustion became a limit Alexander could not overcome. Arrian gives Coenus a speech asking him to consider the survivors who wanted to return home, rather than another river to cross.

scenes.title: Boats on the mud
scenes.caption: Near the Indus mouth, the falling tide left vessels stranded. When the water returned, some boats were damaged as they lifted unevenly from the ground, a coastal hazard unfamiliar to many men used to inland rivers.

scenes.title: A base for the fleet
scenes.caption: At Patala, Alexander ordered work on a harbour and dockyard. The river journey was becoming a sea expedition, and the fleet needed repairs, supplies and a place from which Nearchus could prepare to sail.

scenes.title: The distance between water
scenes.caption: The Gedrosian march crossed country where water and supplies could not reliably be found. A long column, baggage animals and people already weakened by the journey had to cover the same exposed ground, with little shelter from the heat.

scenes.title: The water in a helmet
scenes.caption: Arrian tells of a small quantity of water brought to Alexander in a helmet while the army was suffering from thirst. He poured it away where the soldiers could see, refusing a drink that could not be shared with them.

scenes.title: News from the coast
scenes.caption: When Nearchus reached Alexander in Carmania, the land and sea parties could finally compare what had happened to them. His report brought news of the fleet and of a coastline the army crossing the desert had scarcely seen.

scenes.title: A ceremony of alliance
scenes.caption: At Susa, marriages linked Macedonian officers with women from Persian noble families. Arrian describes the ceremony as following Persian custom; it was also an attempt to bind the conquerors to the elite of the empire they had taken.

scenes.title: Boats for another voyage
scenes.caption: In Babylon, preparations continued for an expedition towards Arabia. Ships, crews and harbour works belonged to plans Alexander would not carry out; his death left the army and its commanders facing the question of what came next.
